sections.body:
A medicine pack is a legal document. Every word printed on it is there because a regulator required it, and the layout is nearly the same in every country because the rules were written to make one pack comparable with another.

The front carries the **brand name**, the largest print on the pack. It is a marketing name owned by one company, and it tells you almost nothing about the medicine itself. The generic name is the important one. It is the international, non-proprietary name of the active ingredient, and the same generic name appears on every pack of that substance in every country. Amoxicillin is amoxicillin whether it was made in Vietnam, Germany or India.

Under the brand name comes the **strength**. This is how much active ingredient is in one unit of the medicine: one tablet, one capsule, one 5 mL measure of liquid. Some packs state two strengths, such as 10 mg and 20 mg, and sell both under the same brand name in the same box. Read the strength of the pack in your hand, not the strength printed on the outer box you last saw in the shop.

Then comes the **form**: tablet, capsule, syrup, suspension, injection, cream, drops, patch, inhaler. The form decides how it enters the body and how quickly it acts.

Then the **indication**, the short list of what the medicine is for. It is written for regulators, not for you, and it can sound frightening. Read it as a short answer to one question: what was this pack made to do?

Then the **directions**: how much to take, how often, when, and for how long. This is the part people skip, and it is the part that decides whether the medicine works.

Then the **warnings and side effects**, usually in the leaflet inside the box rather than on the carton. This is where you find the conditions the medicine must not be used in, the interactions with other medicines, and the effects to expect.

Finally the **ingredients**, the **storage instruction**, the **expiry date** and the **marketing authorisation number**, which identifies the pack in the regulator's records and is what you quote if there is a problem.

Read in that order and you know more about the medicine in your hand than most people ever will.
examples: The generic name is the one on the active ingredient line, and it is the same everywhere.
The brand name is on the front; the strength is the line under it.
sections.heading: What a medicine label actually tells you

sections.body:
Two names for one medicine cause most of the confusion at a pharmacy counter, so it is worth separating them clearly.

The **generic name** names the substance itself: the molecule that does the work in your body. It was chosen by an international committee so that the same substance has the same name in every country. Once a name is allocated it is never reused for a different substance. That is why you can read a generic name on a pack in Hanoi and a pharmacist in another country will understand it.

The **brand name** belongs to one company, which registered it as a trademark. The company may have invented the molecule, or it may simply have bought the right to sell a substance made by someone else. Either way, the brand name tells you who sells it and not what it does.

This matters for three practical reasons. First, a generic version usually costs less, and for many medicines there is no meaningful difference between the brand and the generic in how well they work. Second, when you travel or change pharmacies, the generic name is the word that makes the medicine findable. Third, if you take more than one medicine, the pharmacist needs the generic names to check for interactions between them.

Do not assume a brand is stronger. The number on the pack decides that, not the name. And do not assume a cheap version is a different substance. Check the strength and the active ingredient, and only then compare the price.

Some medicines contain more than one active ingredient, and then the pack lists several generic names. A cold and flu remedy may contain paracetamol for the pain, an antihistamine for the runny nose and a decongestant for the blocked nose. This matters because you can easily end up doubling up on the same substance by taking two different products. Paracetamol appears under many names, and so does ibuprofen.

A **combination product** is any pack with more than one active ingredient. Before you take two packs of the same family, check the active ingredients on both. That single habit prevents a common and avoidable overdose.
examples: Please give me the generic version of this, the same active ingredient and strength.
I take paracetamol for the headache, so I will not take this cold remedy as well.
The brand says one thing and the generic says another, so I checked the active ingredient line.
sections.heading: The generic name and the brand name

sections.body:
Numbers on a pack come in three different jobs, and mixing them up is the most common dosing error people make.

Strength is how much active ingredient is in one dose unit. A tablet marked 500 mg contains 500 milligrams of the active ingredient. One gram is 1000 milligrams, and one microgram is a thousandth of a milligram. On packs of thyroid, allergy and some pain medicines you will see micrograms written as mcg or µg, and a pack that says 50 mcg is not the same medicine as one that says 50 mg.

Concentration is how much active ingredient is in a given volume of liquid. The line "100 mg in 5 mL" does not say the whole bottle contains 100 mg. It says that every 5 mL you measure contains 100 mg. If the bottle holds 100 mL, it holds 2000 mg in total, which is twenty doses.

The amount you take is the third number, and it is on the directions line, not on the strength. "Take 10 mg twice a day" tells you how much. The strength tells you what each unit contains, and you may need more than one unit.

One more number matters more than people expect: the **total quantity in the pack**. A box of twenty 10 mg tablets contains 200 mg in total. A syrup of 100 mL at 100 mg in 5 mL contains 2000 mg in total. This is the number you need when someone has taken too much and the emergency service asks what was swallowed. Find it before you need it, and write it down.

And check the dose unit. Two tablets of 500 mg are 1000 mg, which is a dose of one 1000 mg tablet. But two capsules of 250 mg/5 mL suspension are 500 mg of liquid, and that is not the same thing at all. Always count the milligrams, not the pieces.
examples: This liquid is 100 mg in 5 mL, so 10 mL is 200 mg.
The pack holds twenty 10 mg tablets, so there are 200 mg in total.
The strength is 50 mcg, not 50 mg, so I will check the dose with you.
sections.heading: What 5 mg and per 5 mL actually mean

sections.body:
A medicine can be the right one at the wrong time and still fail. The timing instructions are short, and each one has a meaning.

Once daily means once in each 24-hour period. **Twice daily** means twice in each 24-hour period, and **three times daily** means three times in each 24-hour period. These are clock times, not meals: they do not automatically mean morning, lunch and evening.

Every eight hours is different from three times a day. Three times a day can mean 8 a.m., 1 p.m. and 6 p.m., which leaves only five hours before the last dose. Every eight hours spreads the doses evenly. The same goes for every six hours and every twelve hours. If the pack says every eight hours, keep to eight hours.

Before food means roughly an hour before a meal. **With food** means during or straight after eating, which usually slows the medicine down and reduces stomach upset. **After food** means once the meal is finished. **Empty stomach** usually means one hour before eating or two hours after.

As needed, printed on the label as **PRN** for the Latin *pro re nata*, means take it when the symptom appears, up to the maximum stated. That maximum is a hard limit, not a suggestion. If the pack says no more than eight tablets in 24 hours, then eight is the ceiling whether or not the pain is still bad.

Some medicines must not be stopped suddenly. Corticosteroids, some blood pressure medicines and some antidepressants have to be reduced step by step, because the body has adapted to them. Stopping a course of steroids early because you feel better is a common and avoidable mistake.

And the **missed dose** rule differs between medicines. Some say skip it and take the next one at the usual time. Some say take it as soon as you remember, unless it is nearly time for the next one. Some say never take a double dose. Find that line on your leaflet, because the wrong choice here is one of the few genuinely dangerous ones.
examples: The pack says every eight hours, so I set three alarms for the day.
It says as needed, up to eight tablets in 24 hours, so that is my limit.
I missed the evening dose, so I will take the next one at the usual time.
I have been on this steroid for three weeks, so I will ask how to stop it.
sections.heading: The timing words that decide whether it works

sections.body: Never double a missed dose unless the leaflet explicitly says to. Never share a medicine, even one that was prescribed to you years ago and has no effect now; what is safe for one person can be dangerous for another, and the reasons are often invisible. Check the expiry date before every course, because the date on the outer box may be earlier than the date on the individual blister strip. Keep the leaflet, because the answers to almost every question you will have later are printed inside it. And measure liquid medicines with the device supplied in the pack, never with a kitchen spoon.
sections.heading: Five habits that make a dose unsafe

sections.body:
Liquid medicines fail in one specific way more often than any other: the dose is measured with the wrong thing.

A **measuring spoon** comes in the pack, or the pharmacist will give you one. Use it. It is sized in millilitres, and a level 5 mL spoon is exactly one small medicinal spoonful.

A **household teaspoon** is not a medicinal teaspoon. Kitchen spoons vary in size, and the difference between a 2.5 mL teaspoon and a 5 mL teaspoon is a factor of two. The same is true of tablespoons. If you have to use a kitchen spoon, measure the liquid into the medicinal spoon first and use only that.

A **plastic syringe** is the most accurate method for small doses, and it is worth asking for one for a child, for a medicine measured in millilitres, or for anything with a strong effect such as morphine, insulin or anti-epileptic medicine. Oral syringes have markings in millilitres and there is no confusion with a kitchen spoon. A **dropper** is used for eye drops, ear drops and some liquid medicines, and the drops are not the same size in every product. Count the drops the leaflet tells you to count, not the drops you would pour from a different bottle.

For tablets, the question of crushing matters. Only crush a tablet if the pharmacist or the leaflet tells you it is safe. You must never crush an **enteric-coated** tablet, because the coating is there to release the medicine in the gut rather than the stomach. You must never crush a **modified-release** or **extended-release** tablet, because the coating controls how fast the dose is released. Some medicines are dangerous to handle, and pharmacists will say so.

And check the dose against what is physically in the pack. If the directions say one tablet and the blister holds half-tablet scores, the direction may have changed for the strength you now hold.
examples: I use the syringe that came with the bottle, so the dose is exactly 2.5 mL.
I will not crush this one, because it is enteric-coated.
The directions say one tablet, and the blister has half tablets, so I will check with the pharmacist.
sections.heading: Measuring a dose properly

sections.body:
These are the words you will meet on the pack and in the leaflet, and what each one actually obliges the maker or the pharmacist to do.

Active ingredient is the substance that produces the effect. Everything else in the pack is there to make it stable, palatable, or easy to swallow. **Excipients** are those other substances: fillers, binders, colouring, flavouring. Some people react to an excipient, and that reaction is real even though the ingredient is not the medicine.

Indication is what the medicine is approved to treat. **Contraindication** is a condition in which the medicine must not be used, such as a penicillin allergy or pregnancy. **Side effect** is any effect other than the intended one. **Interaction** is what happens when this medicine meets another one, or food, or alcohol.

Tolerance is when the body gets used to a medicine and the same dose has less effect. **Dependence** is the body's physical need for the substance, which is different from addiction and is why some medicines must be tapered.

Storage gives the temperature and light conditions the medicine needs. A fridge symbol with 2 °C to 8 °C means the medicine belongs in a refrigerator, not in a cupboard and not in a door of the fridge where the temperature moves. **Expiry date** is the last date on which the maker guarantees the medicine will keep its strength and its safety.

Marketing authorisation number is the licence under which the medicine is sold. It is the number to quote in a complaint, and it tells you which country licensed it.
sections.heading: The words on a medicine label, one by one

terms.example: The active ingredient is the same in both packs, only the strength differs.
terms.gloss: The substance in the medicine that produces the effect. Every other substance in the pack is only there to help it.

terms.example: Pregnancy is a contraindication for this medicine, so I will ask about an alternative.
terms.gloss: A condition in which the medicine must not be used, because the risk outweighs the benefit.

terms.example: Nausea is listed as a side effect, and it usually passes after the first few days.
terms.gloss: Any effect the medicine has other than the one it is meant to produce.

terms.example: There is an interaction with this antibiotic, so I will tell the pharmacist about everything I take.
terms.gloss: What happens when a medicine meets another medicine, or alcohol, or a particular food. Some are dangerous.

terms.example: The expiry date is on the strip, so I checked the one on the box too.
terms.gloss: The last date on which the maker guarantees the medicine keeps its strength and its safety.

terms.example: The marketing authorisation number is printed at the bottom of the carton, and I quoted it in the report.
terms.gloss: The licence number under which the medicine is sold. It identifies the pack in the regulator's records.

sections.body:
The leaflet lists every side effect that was reported during testing. That list is longer than any medicine deserves, because a single report counts. So the useful question is not whether a side effect is listed, but how common it is and what you should do about it.

Common effects are usually mild and often settle in the first few days as your body adjusts: nausea, a mild headache, a loose stomach, feeling a little sleepy. **Uncommon** effects are less frequent and more likely to need attention. **Rare** effects are the ones that make people read the leaflet with a pen in their hand.

Some side effects are not really side effects at all but instructions in disguise. "Take with food" usually means the medicine irritates an empty stomach. "May cause drowsiness" usually means do not drive or operate machinery until you know how it affects you. "Expect flushing" is there so that you do not think something is wrong.

Some effects mean stop and get help: swelling of the face, lips or tongue, difficulty breathing, a widespread rash, or a racing heartbeat. These are signs of a serious reaction, and they need emergency care, not another dose.

Interactions are the part people skip, and they are where the real risks sit. Tell the pharmacist about every medicine you take, including the ones you bought yourself, the herbal ones, and the ones you take only occasionally. Most pharmacies keep a record of your purchases, but do not rely on it. The interaction that catches people out most often is between a medicine and alcohol, and it is not always the sleepy one: some medicines cause severe flushing and palpitations with alcohol, and some antibiotics do not work at all if you drink.

If you take a regular medicine, a **medicine review** once a year is worth the appointment. Bring every pack, including the ones you only use now and then. Things that were fine at one dose may not be fine at another, and what is safe with one condition may not be safe with a new one.
examples: It says may cause drowsiness, so I will not drive this evening.
I also take a supplement for my joints, so I will mention it.
I have brought every pack I take, including the ones I use only occasionally.
sections.heading: Side effects, warnings, and what to do about them

sections.body: Some of the important information on a medicine pack is printed as a sign rather than as a sentence, and the signs are the same across most countries. Learn these and you can read a pack you have never seen before.
sections.heading: The marks on the pack

symbols.meaning: OTC: sold without a prescription in a pharmacy, which does not mean it is harmless.
Rx only: this medicine may only be supplied against a valid prescription.
Keep out of the reach of children: the usual mark on every pack sold to the public.
Protect from light: store the pack away from direct sunlight.
Do not crush: the tablet must be swallowed whole.
Refrigerate at 2 °C to 8 °C: the medicine belongs in a refrigerator, not in a cupboard.
Controlled drug: a stricter record is kept and the prescription rules are tighter.
A crossed-out disposal bin: do not throw the pack in household rubbish, take it to a pharmacy take-back point.

sections.body: Six minutes of reading at the counter saves weeks of confusion at home. Run the same routine every time you accept a new pack, whether it was prescribed or bought over the counter.
examples: Before I leave, I want to check the active ingredient and the strength.
Can you show me the leaflet, and where is the missed-dose rule?
sections.heading: A routine for every new medicine you are given
steps: Read the active ingredient and check it is what you expect.
Check the strength, the form and the dose unit.
Read the directions: how much, how often, when, and for how long.
Find the missed-dose rule and write it on the pack.
Find the expiry date and the storage instruction.
Ask the pharmacist the four questions that are left.

sections.body:
A pharmacist is the most reachable health professional you will ever meet. There is no appointment, there is usually no charge, and they see more medicine problems in a day than a doctor does. Most people use this service for one question a year, when they should be using it for every new pack.

Ask **closed** questions when you can, because closed questions get straight answers. "Is this the same as the paracetamol I already take?" gets a yes or no. "Is this the same as my cold medicine?" gets a lecture. "Can I take this with my other tablets?" gets a clear answer you can act on.

The four questions worth asking every time are simple. **What is this medicine for, in one sentence?** **How and when do I take it, and what should I avoid while I take it?** **What should I do if I miss a dose?** **What should make me stop and call you?**

And ask the last question twice, because it is the one nobody asks. If you have to make a phone call to the practice at eleven at night, you want to know in advance which symptoms are worth it.

You do not need to feel foolish at the counter. Pharmacists deal with the same questions every day, and the questions are usually about something that genuinely matters rather than something trivial. It is far better to ask a question that seems obvious than to take a medicine for a month in the wrong way.

Ask again later too. Bodies change, other medicines get added, and a dose that was right for you two years ago may not be right now. The leaflet you were given on the first day is still the leaflet with the answers, and it is worth re-reading when something changes.
examples: Is this the same as the paracetamol I already take at night?
What should I avoid while I take this?
What should make me stop and call you?
Can I take this together with my blood pressure tablets?
sections.heading: Asking the pharmacist, and asking again later

item.summary: A medicine label tells you what is in the pack, how much is in one dose, and when to take it. After reading this you can read any medicine label in any country, measure a dose accurately, spot the instructions people most often ignore, and ask a pharmacist the questions that make the medicine work properly.
item.title: Understanding Medicine Labels and Dosage Instructions
